items.title: Sir Nigel
items.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
items.content:
Nigel Loring, the last offspring of a noble and once thriving line of warriors, struggles, along with his grandmother, to maintain their dwindling estate. Nigel dreams of becoming a knight and performing honorable deeds, but has no means to equip himself. Through some luck and skill, he soon comes to possess a powerful warhorse and a suit of armor. He attaches himself as squire to an old family friend who is going to the wars in France. Before leaving the shores of England, Nigel pledges to his beloved that he will not return to claim her for his bride until he has performed three great deeds.

The adventure moves from England to war on the sea, and then to France. In the face of much danger, the company of knights is always looking to do worshipful acts to bring honor upon themselves, and they are always guided by the highest ideals of chivalry.

was first published serially in 1905. It is a prequel to , and takes place at the outset of the Hundred Years’ War.

items.title: The Cave Girl
items.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
items.content:
Waldo Emerson Smith-Jones is the sheltered, overly educated son of a prominent Boston family. During a voyage to the South Seas, he’s swept overboard, becoming a castaway on a secluded island. He soon he becomes enamored with a local woman, and must learn how to survive in the harsh, uncivilized island environment before he can return to civilization.

Like other Edgar Rice Burroughs works, was first serialized in periodicals before being published as a single volume. The first part of the story was titled “The Cave Girl” and was serialized in in 1913; the second part, titled “The Cave Man,” was serialized in in 1917.

items.title: With Edged Tools
items.author: Henry Seton Merriman
items.content:
Jack Meredith is the scion of a respected family and the beau-ideal of London society; Guy Oscard has chosen to forsake that society for the lonely existence of a big game hunter. Each is now driven by love and pride to seek his fortune in West Africa, where they join a partnership to supply the world’s rarest medicine—a drug derived from the leaves of plant which grows only on a single plateau in the interior of one of the most inaccessible, dangerous places on Earth. These two resourceful men, different though they seem, are united by strength of character and a shared sense of honor. They soon form a friendship which can survive any challenge, whether it be hostile tribesmen, the relentless power of nature, disease, or privation—but which may be destroyed by a secret awaiting them back at home.

in a sense made Henry Seton Merriman’s name as one of the Victorian era’s leading novelists. It showcases his ability to blend several genres—realism, romance, adventure, intrigue, social commentary—into a cohesive, fast-paced story which moved effortlessly from locale to locale and character to character. Unlike many contemporary novelists, Merriman was able to craft supporting characters and themes as memorable as his primary ones, and in he is able to highlight the tensions between the old class structures of England and its rising commercial class consciousness. Against that backdrop is played out a drama in which those embodying the old ways and those embracing the new all demonstrate that strength of character and sense of honor transcend any narrow sense of class.

items.title: The Gold Bag
items.author: Carolyn Wells
items.content:
Detective Herbert Burroughs is called to West Sedgwick to investigate the murder of Joseph Crawford, a wealthy man found shot in his own home. The most substantial piece of evidence is a gold bag which has been left at the scene of the crime.

Among the suspects are Crawford’s niece Florence Lloyd and her fiancé Gregory Hall—a liaison which Crawford disapproved of. Before his death, Crawford often threatened to remove Lloyd from his will unless she broke off her engagement to Hall, and Crawford was in fact already in the process of doing so at the time of his death.

During his investigation, Burroughs rapidly falls in love with Lloyd and tries to prove her innocence, while remaining suspicious of Hall, who repeatedly refuses to provide an alibi for where he was the night of the crime. After following seemingly every possible clue to the killer’s identity, Herbert Burroughs’ idol, Fleming Stone, a master of deduction, is called upon to help solve this difficult case.

items.title: The Green Mummy
items.author: Fergus Hume
items.content:
Archie Hope seeks to marry the delightful Lucy Kendal, the stepdaughter of Professor Braddock, an eccentric Egyptology enthusiast. Archie tries to gain Braddock’s approval by purchasing for him a rare Peruvian mummy—yet far from bringing a joyful resolution to Archie’s dilemma, the mummy’s arrival heralds murder and mystery. Plunged into chaos, the young couple and their friends must race to unravel a crime and uncover a missing fortune in Incan emeralds.

Blending classic detective fiction with light romance, is a classic tale from the prolific Fergus Hume. By weaving popular Victorian sensibilities with the era’s fascination with antiquity and Egyptology, Hume delivers an engaging story of murder, greed, and suspense.

items.title: The Prisoner in the Opal
items.author: A. E. W. Mason
items.content:
A pretty American implores wine enthusiast Ricardo to alter his plans for an upcoming visit to vineyards in France to protect her friend, who she fears is threatened by ominous occult forces. He tries to evade responsibility, only to find that his plans have been switched for him. Thrust unanticipated among unfamiliar guests at the chateau, including, unexpectedly, the pretty American, he witnesses odd events and senses sinister intrigue. The uneasy gathering erupts into chaos when two young women vanish.

Famous Parisian detective Inspector Hanaud is in the area investigating a series of young women gone missing, and now he’s faced with another disappearance and a murder. Confusing clues are gathered from detective work, coincidences, and chance conversations, while complex characters who hide secrets ranging from amusing to insidious to satanic rotate into the picture. Hanaud desperately tries to prevent another murder of a witness as the group races to find her.

items.title: Short Fiction
items.author: John Buchan
items.content:
Though perhaps better known as a novelist, John Buchan was also a prolific author of short fiction, having published several short stories and collections during his life.

A Scotsman, many of Buchan’s stories are set in Scotland and feature regional folklore and customs of the region, often making use of Scottish vernacular speech. His writes in many genres, including adventure and historical fiction, and covers many themes, like spirituality and the supernatural.

items.title: Ivanov
items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.content:
The titular Ivanov is a landowner who once loved life, but is now deeply depressed and listless. His wife Anna Petrovna is a Jewish woman who was disinherited by her parents after joining the Russian Church to marry him. She’s dying of tuberculosis, and her doctor, Yevgeny Konstantinovitch Lvov, begs Ivanov to take her to Crimea to help her recover. When Ivanov refuses, Lvov begins to believe that Ivanov is a horrible man—and wants to expose him so that everyone else thinks so, too.

Meanwhile, Ivanov is deeply in debt to the wife of his good friend, the District Chairman Pavel Kirillitch Lebedyev. Despite this, Ivanov continues to thwart this estate manager’s schemes to make more money. Meanwhile Sasha, the Lebedyev’s daughter, becomes infatuated with Ivanov, and works to save him from the black cloud that is slowly enveloping him.

Some want Ivanov to be happy; others want him to be miserable. But in the end, Ivanov will choose his own fate.

is a deep exploration of how a human being is perceived by others and themselves. As Ivanov says to Lvov: “Man is such a simple, uncomplicated machine. … No, doctor, there are too many wheels and screws and levers in any one of us for us to be able to judge each other from the first impression or from two or three external signs. I don’t understand you, you don’t understand me, and we don’t understand ourselves.”

was first performed in 1887, but was not a success. Chekhov made changes as a result, and when it was performed again in 1889, it was much more well-received.

items.title: Short Fiction
items.author: Joseph Conrad
items.content:
Joseph Conrad, the Polish-born writer who published exclusively in English, is known as much for his short fiction as for his novels. Almost all of his stories were first serialized in periodicals such as , , and . They were later republished in seven collections: , Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories, Typhoon and Other Stories, , , , and . Many of his stories deal with the sea and exotic locales (the Malay Archipelago, Central Africa, South America), while others reflect his wider interests, such as his fascination with the Napoleonic era.

Conrad’s most famous novella contained in this collection, “Heart of Darkness,” was originally published serially as a three-part story. It is a short but thematically complex novella exploring colonialism, humanity, and what constitutes a savage society. Set in the Congo in Central Africa, the tale is told in the frame of the recollections of one Charles Marlow, a captain of an ivory steamer. Marlow’s search for the mysterious and powerful “first-class agent” Kurtz gives way to a nuanced and powerful commentary on the horrors of colonialism, called by some the most analyzed work at university-level instruction.

Other notable works include “An Outpost of Progress,” a precursor to “Heart of Darkness,” “Youth,” based on Conrad’s own maritime experiences, “Typhoon,” in which a stubborn captain takes on a force of nature, “The Duel,” later filmed by Ridley Scott as “The Duellists,” and “The Secret Sharer,” in which a captain harbors a fugitive. This collection comprises all the short stories and novellas from Conrad’s seven short fiction collections, plus “The Sisters,” an unfinished short story published posthumously. They’re arranged in order of first publication, which in most cases means their magazine serialization.

items.title: The Vultures
items.author: Henry Seton Merriman
items.content:
In , Henry Seton Merriman plots a taut, fast-moving story of international intrigue which seems as though it could’ve been written in the modern era rather than in the Victorian.

Reginald Cartoner, a British agent, and his counterpart in the French service, Paul Deulin, have worked with and against one another for many years, building a mutual professional respect and a wary friendship. They and an American, Joseph Mangles, are known by political insiders as “vultures”—men whose sudden arrival in a seemingly peaceful place presages the end of that calm and the start of a crisis which will command the world’s attention. All three have just arrived in Warsaw, the principal city of what was formerly a free Polish state but which is now brutally controlled by the Russian Empire of Tsar Aleksandr II.

Prince Bukaty, his son Prince Martin, and his daughter Princess Wanda, whose power and wealth were stripped by the Russians decades earlier, maintain their connections throughout Europe and secretly lay the groundwork for revolt; in this they’re joined by the radical Kosmaroff, whose origins are as mysterious as his methods are ruthless. As the Polish people await the trigger for their revolution, they’re uncertain whether the three vultures have been sent to aid, to oppose, or to simply observe them, or even whether the three are cooperating or at cross-purposes with one another. As personal connections amongst all of the players are strained by conflicting duties and national loyalties, their situation in Poland becomes more perilous by the moment.
